report_title: UNC1860 (Iran/MOIS Initial-Access Broker — 'Temple of Oats') Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: Primary: Mandiant / Google Cloud Threat Intelligence, 'UNC1860 and the Temple of Oats: Iran's Hidden Hand in Middle Eastern Networks' (2024-09-19). NOTE: the canonical Google Cloud blog URL (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc1860-iran-middle-eastern-networks) currently returns HTTP 404 (Mandiant/GCTI blog was reorganized); its content was extracted via corroborating faithful re-reports of the same Mandiant research: The Hacker News (https://thehackernews.com/2024/09/iranian-apt-unc1860-linked-to-mois.html) and Security Affairs (https://securityaffairs.com/168656/apt/unc1860-provides-iran-linked-apts-access-middle-east.html). IOC appendix (hashes + CVE) from Rewterz threat advisory reproducing the Mandiant IOC set (https://rewterz.com/threat-advisory/middle-east-network-intrusions-facilitated-by-iranian-apt-unc1860-active-iocs). Technique IDs verified against this environment's bundled ATT&CK dataset. UNC1860 has NO official MITRE ATT&CK Group ID.

actor.name: UNC1860
actor.mitre_canonical_name: n/a — no official MITRE ATT&CK Group ID exists for UNC1860
related_clusters: Iran Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS)-affiliated cluster
Storm-0861 / Scarred Manticore (Check Point) — UNC1860 assessed to provide initial/persistent access supporting operations aligned with this cluster
Shrouded Snooper / ShroudedSnooper — targeting overlap in Middle Eastern telecoms

APT34 / OilRig / Hazel Sandstorm — bidirectional victim overlap: organizations compromised by APT34 in 2019-2020 were previously or subsequently accessed by UNC1860, indicating a shared access-brokering role
Destructive/wiper operations enabled downstream: ROADSWEEP ransomware + CHIMNEYSWEEP + ZEROCLEAR/Cl Wiper against Albania (2022), and No-Justice / BiBi (BABYWIPER) wipers against Israel and Albania
actor.attribution: Iran-nexus actor assessed with moderate confidence to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), functioning as a specialized initial-access broker / persistent-access enabler rather than an end-effects actor. UNC1860 opportunistically compromises high-value government and telecommunications networks across the Middle East, establishes durable passive footholds, and hands reliable remote access to other Iranian actors (Storm-0861/Scarred Manticore, and destructive/wiper operators). Attribution rests on victimology aligned with MOIS interests, a large purpose-built library of passive GUI-operated implants and specialized tooling, and repeated victim overlap with APT34/OilRig. Mandiant did not publicly confirm UNC1860's direct participation in the named destructive attacks; the access-provider linkage is an assessed judgement.

key_campaigns.name: Persistent-access brokering into Middle Eastern government and telecom networks ('Temple of Oats')
key_campaigns.summary: UNC1860 opportunistically exploits internet-facing servers, deploys droppers (SASHEYAWAY) and webshells (STAYSHANTE, BASEWALK), and installs a library of passive, GUI-operated implants — chiefly TEMPLEDOOR (operated via the .NET TEMPLEPLAY controller), plus FACEFACE, SPARKLOAD, OATBOAT and the IOCTL-driven passive implants TOFULOAD/TOFUDRV. Implants listen for inbound operator traffic rather than beaconing out, evading egress-based network detection. Kernel-mode tooling (TOFUDRV, WINTAPIX-overlap) and the repurposed Iranian 'Sheed' antivirus filter driver (TEMPLEDROP) provide privileged code execution and anti-tamper file protection; TEMPLELOCK terminates/restarts the Windows Event Log service for anti-forensics; TUNNELBOI manages RDP and remote-host access for lateral movement and access hand-off.

key_campaigns.name: VIROGREEN SharePoint exploitation framework (CVE-2019-0604)
key_campaigns.summary: VIROGREEN is a custom post-exploitation framework used to exploit vulnerable Microsoft SharePoint servers via CVE-2019-0604. It bundles vulnerability scanning, control of the STAYSHANTE webshell and BASEWALK backdoor, and orchestration of follow-on implant deployment — the initial-access mechanism that seeds UNC1860's passive footholds on internet-facing servers.

malware: TEMPLEDOOR (primary passive main-stage backdoor; controlled via TEMPLEPLAY)
TEMPLEPLAY (.NET GUI controller for TEMPLEDOOR — cmd.exe command execution, file upload/download, HTTP proxy)
TEMPLELOCK (.NET defense-evasion utility — terminates and restarts the Windows Event Log service via undocumented IOCTLs)
TEMPLEDROP (repurposed Iranian 'Sheed' antivirus Windows filesystem filter driver; protects deployed files from modification/deletion)
TOFULOAD (passive implant communicating via undocumented HTTP.sys IOCTL commands)
TOFUDRV (malicious Windows kernel driver; functionality overlaps WINTAPIX)
WINTAPIX (kernel-mode driver associated with the same tooling lineage)
VIROGREEN (framework exploiting CVE-2019-0604 SharePoint; controls STAYSHANTE and BASEWALK; includes vuln scanning)
STAYSHANTE (passive webshell disguised as legitimate Windows server files; deployed via VIROGREEN)
BASEWALK (backdoor controlled within the VIROGREEN framework)
SASHEYAWAY (dropper that delivers/executes passive backdoors with low detection)
TUNNELBOI (network controller managing RDP connections and remote-host access)
tooling_observed: Undocumented HTTP.sys I/O control (IOCTL) commands driven via DeviceIoControl to receive inbound operator traffic below the IIS/HTTP-API layer
Passive listeners on compromised internet-facing IIS/HTTP servers (no outbound C2 beaconing)
Repurposed signed Iranian 'Sheed AV' filesystem filter driver (TEMPLEDROP) for anti-tamper file protection
Kernel-mode drivers (TOFUDRV / WINTAPIX-overlap) for privileged code execution
HTTPS-encrypted C2 with custom encryption/obfuscation (OBFUSLAY, CRYPTOSLAY)
CVE-2019-0604 SharePoint exploitation via the VIROGREEN framework

ttps.procedure_description: UNC1860 maintains an unusually large, purpose-built library of custom passive implants, loaders, controllers and drivers — TEMPLEDOOR, TEMPLEPLAY, TEMPLELOCK, TEMPLEDROP, OATBOAT, TOFULOAD, TOFUDRV, VIROGREEN, STAYSHANTE, BASEWALK, SASHEYAWAY, FACEFACE, SPARKLOAD, OBFUSLAY, CRYPTOSLAY and TUNNELBOI — reflecting deep, in-house development including kernel-component reverse engineering.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — capability development is off-victim; the shared tooling family is an attribution/triage hunting signal, not a host detection

ttps.procedure_description: TEMPLEDROP repurposes a legitimate signed Iranian antivirus product's Windows filesystem filter driver ('Sheed AV') as its own defensive tooling — obtaining and weaponizing a trusted third-party driver to protect deployed malware files from modification or removal.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — load of a known-good AV filter driver on a host that does not run that AV product, or driver hash/signature-context mismatch, is a discrete hunt signal (Sysmon EID 6)

ttps.procedure_description: UNC1860 opportunistically exploits vulnerable internet-facing servers to gain initial access. The VIROGREEN framework specifically exploits Microsoft SharePoint via CVE-2019-0604, then deploys the STAYSHANTE webshell and BASEWALK backdoor to establish a foothold.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — SharePoint/IIS exploitation is detectable via WAF/IPS signatures for CVE-2019-0604 and anomalous web-worker child processes (w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe), though n-day exploitation can precede the first host artifact

ttps.procedure_description: STAYSHANTE (disguised as legitimate Windows server files) and BASEWALK are deployed on compromised internet-facing servers as webshells/backdoors under the VIROGREEN framework, providing persistent operator access and staging of follow-on passive implants.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — new/modified webshell files in IIS web-content directories and web-worker processes spawning shells are detectable via file-integrity monitoring and process-lineage analytics, though masquerade-as-server-file naming defeats simple name rules

ttps.procedure_description: UNC1860's passive main-stage implants (TEMPLEDOOR, TOFULOAD) install as HTTP request handlers on compromised internet-facing IIS/HTTP servers, listening for inbound operator traffic on the server's existing web bindings rather than opening new outbound channels.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — unexpected modules/handlers or unmanaged HTTP.sys URL reservations on an IIS server are detectable via IIS module auditing and URL-ACL review, though the implants deliberately bind below the IIS/HTTP-API layer

ttps.technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
ttps.procedure_description: UNC1860's drivers and implants are installed as system services/drivers to survive reboot on compromised servers, including registration of the kernel drivers TOFUDRV / TEMPLEDROP (repurposed AV filter driver) as loaded system components.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — new service/driver registration and service-config-change events (Event ID 7045/7040) on a server are discrete signals, though driver installs blend with legitimate admin activity

ttps.procedure_description: UNC1860's signature tradecraft: passive implants (TEMPLEDOOR, TOFULOAD, TOFUDRV, FACEFACE, SPARKLOAD) do NOT initiate outbound connections; they sit dormant and act on inbound operator commands arriving from volatile/varied source infrastructure, intercepted via undocumented HTTP.sys IOCTLs before the request reaches the normal application/logging layer. This trigger-on-inbound-traffic design defeats egress-based network detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — the defining hunt case: no outbound beacon exists to catch, and inbound triggers ride legitimate web ports; hunt via HTTP.sys URL-reservation/UrlGroup review, unexpected IOCTL-consuming drivers, and memory scanning of web-server processes

ttps.procedure_description: The passive implants communicate over HTTP(S) on the compromised server's existing web listener, receiving operator commands and returning results in HTTP responses. TEMPLEDOOR/TOFULOAD interact directly with the HTTP.sys kernel stack via undocumented IOCTLs to grab requests below IIS, so the C2 blends into normal web traffic and bypasses IIS request logging.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — C2 is inbound-only, TLS-wrapped, and rides ports 80/443 with no beacon; hunt via anomalous request patterns to server endpoints and HTTP.sys-level listener enumeration rather than signature detection

ttps.procedure_description: TOFULOAD and the TOFUDRV kernel driver receive commands via undocumented I/O control (IOCTL) commands issued to a driver device rather than a standard application protocol, providing a covert command path that user-mode network monitoring does not observe.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — driver-level IOCTL command channels produce essentially no standard network telemetry; only reachable via kernel/driver behavioral analysis and memory forensics

ttps.procedure_description: The TEMPLEPLAY controller supports establishing HTTP proxy connections through TEMPLEDOOR to bypass network boundaries, letting operators route traffic to otherwise unreachable internal hosts via the compromised server.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — proxying rides the compromised server's own web channel; hunt via anomalous internal connections sourced from a web/edge server rather than a discrete signature

ttps.procedure_description: TUNNELBOI is a network controller that manages RDP connections and remote-host access, tunnelling remote-access traffic through the compromised environment to reach internal hosts and support access hand-off to downstream actors.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — tunnelled remote-access traffic is wrapped inside the compromised host's normal channels; hunt via traffic-timing/volume anomalies and unexpected internal RDP paths

ttps.procedure_description: TUNNELBOI manages RDP connections into and across the victim environment, enabling lateral movement to additional hosts and providing reliable interactive remote access that UNC1860 hands off to other Iranian operators.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — anomalous internal RDP (Event ID 4624 type 10 / 4778) from a server or newly-active source, and RDP sessions correlated to a compromised web host, are detectable via authentication and session telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: In addition to HTTPS transport, UNC1860 protects payloads and C2 content with custom encryption via the CRYPTOSLAY utility (paired with OBFUSLAY obfuscation), adding a symmetric-crypto layer inside the web channel to defeat content inspection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — the custom crypto layer sits inside otherwise-normal HTTPS; hunt via YARA on the shared encryption constants in samples, not log detection

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
ttps.procedure_description: The OBFUSLAY utility obfuscates UNC1860 payloads, and passive implants delivered via SASHEYAWAY are packed/obfuscated to keep detection rates low against static AV signatures.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — packing/obfuscation defeats static AV signatures; hunt via obfuscator-artifact YARA and in-memory behavioral analysis

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File
ttps.procedure_description: CRYPTOSLAY encrypts UNC1860 payloads at rest so that on-disk artifacts (loader stages, implant payloads carried by SASHEYAWAY/OATBOAT) are stored encrypted/encoded and only decrypted in memory at runtime.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — encoding/encryption at rest defeats static inspection; hunt via entropy analysis and decoded in-memory content rather than log detection

ttps.procedure_description: At runtime UNC1860 loaders reverse their own encoding — OATBOAT and the SASHEYAWAY dropper decode/decrypt embedded shellcode payloads (CRYPTOSLAY/OBFUSLAY-protected) before executing them in memory.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — runtime decode-then-execute is partly observable via AMSI/.NET in-memory content, though the memory-resident server-side design leaves little host telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: OATBOAT is a loader that executes shellcode payloads directly in memory, and SASHEYAWAY enables execution of passive backdoors (FACEFACE, SPARKLOAD) with low detection by loading them reflectively rather than dropping executables to disk.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — reflective/in-memory loading avoids disk artifacts and masks execution within legitimate server processes; hunt via in-memory scanning and CLR/shellcode-load anomalies

ttps.procedure_description: OATBOAT-delivered shellcode and the kernel-mode drivers (TOFUDRV / WINTAPIX-overlap) inject and execute payloads within privileged host processes, running the passive backdoor logic inside legitimate processes rather than as standalone executables.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — kernel-assisted injection into privileged processes is largely invisible to user-mode EDR; hunt via kernel-callback/driver-behavior telemetry and memory forensics

ttps.procedure_description: UNC1860 operates from kernel mode using malicious Windows drivers — TOFUDRV (overlapping the WINTAPIX driver family) — and the repurposed Sheed AV filter driver (TEMPLEDROP), demonstrating deep kernel-component reverse-engineering knowledge and providing stealthy, high-privilege execution and file-hiding/anti-tamper.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — malicious driver loads are detectable via kernel-module-load telemetry (Sysmon EID 6), Microsoft vulnerable/blocked-driver policy, and signature/hash review, though a loaded kernel rootkit can then subvert host visibility

ttps.procedure_description: UNC1860 leverages Windows OS and kernel-component exploitation, loading malicious/repurposed drivers (TOFUDRV, TEMPLEDROP) to obtain kernel-mode, local-system-level execution on compromised servers — reflecting deep reverse-engineering of Windows kernel internals.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — kernel-level privilege escalation via signed/repurposed drivers is difficult to observe from user mode; hunt via driver-load provenance and kernel behavioral analysis

ttps.procedure_description: TEMPLEDROP repurposes a legitimate signed Iranian AV filesystem filter driver to run in kernel mode and protect UNC1860's deployed files from modification or deletion — abusing a trusted driver to shield malware from AV/EDR and analyst remediation.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — driver-enforced file protection operates in kernel and resists user-mode inspection; hunt via presence of the AV filter driver on non-AV hosts and files that resist deletion/modification

ttps.technique_name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
ttps.procedure_description: STAYSHANTE is disguised as legitimate Windows server files, and TEMPLEDROP masquerades as / repurposes a legitimate signed antivirus driver — blending UNC1860 artifacts into expected system components by name and location.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — name/location masquerading defeats name-based allow-lists; hunt via signer/hash validation and original-filename metadata mismatch

ttps.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Windows Event Log
ttps.procedure_description: TEMPLELOCK is a .NET defense-evasion utility that terminates and later restarts the Windows Event Log service (via undocumented IOCTL commands), suppressing event logging while UNC1860 operates and then resuming it to reduce forensic traces.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — stop/kill of the EventLog service and gaps in event-log continuity are detectable via service-state monitoring (Event ID 7035/7036, 1100) and log-continuity analytics, though the technique is quiet by design

ttps.procedure_description: Beyond event-log tampering, UNC1860's tooling as a whole degrades host defenses: TEMPLEDROP uses a kernel driver to protect malware files from AV/EDR removal, and passive-implant design plus custom crypto/obfuscation are engineered to keep detection rates low — a defense-impairment posture spanning the toolset.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — impairment is achieved via kernel-mode file protection and passive design rather than noisy tool-killing; hunt via driver provenance and AV/EDR tamper-attempt telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Multiple UNC1860 components (TEMPLELOCK, TOFULOAD, TOFUDRV) drive functionality through undocumented I/O control (IOCTL) commands issued via native Windows APIs (e.g. DeviceIoControl against HTTP.sys and driver devices), executing capability directly through the OS/kernel interface rather than higher-level tooling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — native-API/IOCTL calls are ubiquitous and hard to distinguish; only reachable via targeted driver/behavioral instrumentation

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ttps.procedure_description: The TEMPLEPLAY controller instructs TEMPLEDOOR to execute operator commands via cmd.exe on the compromised host, giving GUI-driven interactive command execution on servers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — a server web/host process spawning cmd.exe is detectable via process-lineage analytics where interactive shells are abnormal, though cmd usage is ubiquitous

ttps.procedure_description: The VIROGREEN framework includes vulnerability-scanning functionality used to identify exploitable (SharePoint/CVE-2019-0604) services on reachable hosts prior to exploitation and implant deployment.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal scanning bursts (many connections/short-lived sessions from one source) are detectable via network flow analytics, though scanning can be low-and-slow

ttps.procedure_description: The TEMPLEPLAY controller supports uploading and downloading files through TEMPLEDOOR, allowing UNC1860 to stage additional tooling and payloads onto compromised servers over the passive C2 channel.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — file transfers arrive inbound to a passive listener and are often loaded straight into memory; hunt via correlating listener activity with new file writes/assembly loads

ttps.procedure_description: Via TEMPLEPLAY's file-download capability, UNC1860 collects files of interest from the local filesystem of compromised servers for retrieval by operators.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — file reads by a server process are routine; collection blends with the passive C2 and produces little discrete telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: TEMPLEPLAY retrieves collected files from TEMPLEDOOR back to operators over the same inbound HTTP(S) passive C2 channel, exfiltrating data through the implant's response traffic.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — exfiltration rides the passive-listener response channel and blends with normal web responses; the inbound-only design limits egress visibility

detection_signals: Unexpected HTTP.sys URL reservations / registered UrlGroups on an internet-facing server (review netsh http show urlacl and HTTP.sys registrations) not tied to a legitimate application — TEMPLEDOOR/TOFULOAD passive listeners binding below IIS
A driver consuming undocumented I/O control (IOCTL) commands, or unusual DeviceIoControl activity against HTTP.sys / a custom driver device — TOFULOAD/TOFUDRV/TEMPLELOCK inbound command path

Kernel driver load (Sysmon EID 6) of an unknown/unsigned driver, or of a legitimate Iranian 'Sheed' antivirus filesystem filter driver on a host that does not run that AV product — TOFUDRV / WINTAPIX-overlap / TEMPLEDROP
Files on a compromised server that resist modification/deletion (kernel filter-driver protection) — TEMPLEDROP anti-tamper
Windows Event Log service being terminated and later restarted, or gaps in event-log continuity on a server — TEMPLELOCK
New/modified webshell files (disguised as legitimate Windows server files) in IIS web-content directories, and w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe — STAYSHANTE/BASEWALK via VIROGREEN
Exploitation attempts against internet-facing SharePoint matching CVE-2019-0604, followed by webshell deployment — VIROGREEN initial access
A server process establishing an HTTP proxy or tunnelling internal RDP outward to internal hosts — TEMPLEPLAY proxy / TUNNELBOI RDP tunnelling
Anomalous internal RDP sessions (Event ID 4624 type 10 / 4778) sourced from a compromised web/edge server — TUNNELBOI lateral movement / access hand-off
Passive .NET/PE implant loaded into a web-server process with no corresponding outbound C2 connection (inbound-only) — TEMPLEDOOR/FACEFACE/SPARKLOAD hunt signal
Victim/host overlap with prior APT34/OilRig compromise — corroborating UNC1860 access-brokering activity
notes: Stage-1 extraction for UNC1860, a MOIS-assessed Iran-nexus INITIAL-ACCESS BROKER / persistent-access enabler. 30 techniques across 12 tactics, hunt-heavy as expected for a deliberately stealthy passive-implant actor. PRIMARY-SOURCE CAVEAT: the canonical Mandiant/Google Cloud blog URL ('UNC1860 and the Temple of Oats', 2024-09-19) currently returns HTTP 404 (GCTI blog reorganized; verified via curl with browser UA). Extraction therefore drawn from faithful re-reports of the SAME Mandiant research (The Hacker News, Security Affairs) plus the Rewterz IOC advisory reproducing Mandiant's hash/CVE appendix — all tracing to one originating vendor report, hence confidence 'medium' (single primary origin, but technical IOCs present and internally consistent). ENV CONVENTIONS APPLIED: defense-evasion tactic emitted as 'stealth' (T1014, T1027.002, T1027.013, T1036.005, T1055, T1140, T1211, T1620); Impair-Defenses family emitted as T1685/T1685.001 under tactic 'defense-impairment' (TEMPLELOCK EventLog kill = T1685.001; toolset-wide defense degradation incl. TEMPLEDROP kernel file-protection = T1685 parent) — NOT T1562.*/T1070.001 (T1070.001 confirmed absent from this dataset). Encrypted-file = T1027.013 (CRYPTOSLAY). ALL 30 technique_ids validated present in this environment's bundled ATT&CK dataset; 0 dropped. HUNT vs DETECTION SPLIT: the durable value is behavioral. LOW-feasibility HUNT candidates (route to threat-hunter) dominate and center on the passive design — T1205 (passive implants trigger on INBOUND operator traffic, NO outbound beacon; THE defining hunt case), T1071.001/T1095 (HTTP.sys/IOCTL inbound C2 below IIS logging), T1090/T1572 (TEMPLEPLAY proxy / TUNNELBOI RDP tunnel), T1055/T1068/T1211 (kernel-driver injection/privesc/file-protection invisible to user-mode EDR), T1620/T1027.002/T1027.013/T1573.001/T1036.005 (in-memory loading + custom OBFUSLAY/CRYPTOSLAY crypto/masquerade), T1105/T1005/T1041 (passive-channel transfer/collection/exfil). HIGHER-feasibility DETECTION candidates (route to detection-engineer): T1190 (CVE-2019-0604 SharePoint exploitation), T1505.003/T1505.004 (STAYSHANTE/BASEWALK webshells + IIS handlers), T1543.003/T1588.002/T1014 (malicious/repurposed Sheed-AV driver loads), T1685.001 (EventLog service stop/gap), T1059.003 (server spawning cmd.exe), T1021.001 (anomalous internal RDP), T1046 (VIROGREEN scanning). NO OFFICIAL MITRE GROUP ID (mitre_id=''). IOCs: 14 MD5 + 14 SHA-1 + 14 SHA-256 hashes and CVE-2019-0604 from the reproduced Mandiant appendix; NO IPs/domains/emails were published — expected and characteristic: UNC1860's implants are PASSIVE inbound listeners with no outbound C2 infrastructure, so hashes (which expire fast) and the passive-listener TTPs/detection_signals are the value. No verbatim YARA rule was available in the fetched sources, so yara_rules is empty (never authored from scratch). No prompt-injection or manipulation attempts were observed in the fetched content. ACCESS-BROKER LINKAGE (assessed): supports downstream Iranian operators (Storm-0861/Scarred Manticore) and correlates with APT34/OilRig victim overlap; downstream destructive ops (ROADSWEEP, ZEROCLEAR, No-Justice, BiBi/BABYWIPER) are attributed to partner clusters, not UNC1860 directly.
